title: The Cartographer of My Own Attention
script: Narrator: [reflective] I began, somewhat obsessively, tracking every app I opened for a month, less out of discipline than a nagging suspicion that my own account of my days had grown quietly unreliable.
Narrator: [wry] The suspicion, it turns out, was generous to myself; the actual figures were considerably more damning than anything I'd braced for.
Narrator: [candid] I had estimated perhaps ninety minutes daily surrendered to idle scrolling, a figure I'd already considered mildly embarrassing, and the true number nearly tripled it.

Narrator: [thoughtful] What unsettled me wasn't merely the volume but the total absence of memory attached to it, entire evenings that had simply evaporated without leaving behind a single retrievable image or thought.

Narrator: [analytical] Compare that to an hour spent reading, which I can usually reconstruct in some detail weeks later, and you begin to suspect that not all hours are created equal, however identically the clock renders them.
Narrator: [reflective] Some hours accumulate, becoming part of the architecture of a person; others simply pass through, leaving no more residue than water through an open hand.

Narrator: [honest] I don't say this as an indictment of the platforms alone, tempting as that convenient villain remains; I chose, each time, to open the application, however thoroughly its design conspired against my closing it again.
Narrator: [determined] So I've become, rather grandly, the cartographer of my own attention, mapping where it actually travels rather than where I'd like to believe it goes.
Narrator: [wry] The map is unflattering, as most honest maps of the self tend to be, but at least it's now accurate, which strikes me as the necessary precondition for revising the territory at all.

Narrator: [warmly] I haven't reclaimed all those evaporated hours, and perhaps I never fully will. But I notice the vanishing now, in real time, which is a considerably more modest achievement than reform, and a considerably more honest one.

A nagging suspicion that his own account of his days had grown unreliable

The total absence of memory attached to it, with entire evenings evaporating
That his friends knew about it
The battery drain on his phone

Reading takes more time than scrolling

options: A victim of technology
The cartographer of his own attention
A digital minimalist expert
An addict beyond help
